topic: Sound for Picture — Post Workflow & Deliverables

fields.definition: In sound design, the practice of giving a recorded or synthesized sound a convincing sense of physical mass and force, chiefly by adding low-frequency energy, sub-bass layers, slower attack transients, and low-end resonance so an on-screen object or creature reads as heavy.
fields.plain_english: This means making a sound feel big and heavy. Sound designers add deep, low tones under a sound so a thing on screen seems to have real weight, like a huge door or a giant's footstep.
fields.purpose_function: It sells the size and mass of on-screen objects or creatures whose recorded sounds are too thin, so the audience feels the impact and believes what they see.
fields.practical_application: A designer layers a sub-bass boom or low rumble under a sword swing, punch, or creature step, then shapes the low end with EQ so the hit lands with felt weight in the room.
common_mistakes: Adding so much sub-bass that the mix turns muddy and masks dialogue.
Relying only on low end and forgetting the mid and high crack that gives a hit definition.
Ignoring bass management limits, so weight that felt good in one room overloads or vanishes on other systems.
Using the same low-end layer on every object, so nothing feels distinct.
scenario_contexts: Making a CG creature's footsteps feel massive in a fantasy film.
Beefing up a car-door slam that was recorded too thin.
Giving a punch or body impact felt force in an action scene.

sources: Sonnenschein, Sound Design: The Expressive Power of Music, Voice and Sound Effects in Cinema
Viers, The Sound Effects Bible
Yewdall, Practical Art of Motion Picture Sound

fields.definition: A playback method, common in interactive and game audio engines, in which the system randomly selects one sound from a group of variations each time a cue fires, with each variation given a probability weight so more-likely versions play more often than others.
fields.plain_english: This is a way to stop a sound from getting boring. The computer keeps a small set of versions of a sound and picks one at random each time, but you can make some versions come up more often than others.
fields.purpose_function: It prevents the machine-gun effect of hearing the exact same sample over and over, adding natural variety while still letting the designer favour certain versions.
fields.practical_application: In tools like Wwise or FMOD, a designer drops several footstep or gunshot takes into a random container and sets weights so common variants play often and rare ones only now and then.
common_mistakes: Thinking equal weights and true random are the same, when weighting changes how often each version plays.
Using too few variations, so repetition is still obvious.
Setting one weight so high the other versions almost never play, which defeats the point.
Forgetting to also randomize pitch or volume, so the variants still sound cloned.
scenario_contexts: Randomizing footstep samples so a character's walk never sounds looped.
Varying gunfire or impact hits in a game so they feel alive.
Cycling ambient bird or insect calls in a game environment.

sources: Audiokinetic Wwise documentation (Random Container playback behavior)
FMOD Studio documentation (multi-instrument and playback probability)
Stevens & Raybould, Game Audio Implementation

fields.definition: A designed sound effect marked by a fast rising-and-falling swish of broadband, filtered noise or air-like tone, used to accent rapid motion, transitions, reveals, and fast camera or object moves.
fields.plain_english: A whoosh is that fast swish sound you hear when something flies past or a title zooms onto the screen. Designers often build it from shaped noise or the sound of moving air.
fields.purpose_function: It draws the ear to speed and movement, smooths cuts and transitions, and adds energy to moments the picture alone cannot fully sell.
fields.practical_application: An editor lays a whoosh on a swinging sword, a fast whip-pan, or a logo sting, often pitch-bending or Doppler-processing noise or recorded air to match the on-screen speed.
common_mistakes: Overusing whooshes so every cut has one, which tires the audience.
Leaving the whoosh too loud, so it fights dialogue or music.
Not matching the whoosh timing and direction to the on-screen move.
Using a stock whoosh that clashes with the scene's tone.
scenario_contexts: Accenting a fast camera move or whip-pan.
Adding motion to a title or logo animation.
Emphasizing a fast swing, throw, or punch in an action scene.

sources: Viers, The Sound Effects Bible
Sonnenschein, Sound Design: The Expressive Power of Music, Voice and Sound Effects in Cinema
Yewdall, Practical Art of Motion Picture Sound

fields.definition: In sound editorial and design, a work pass dedicated solely to the wind element of a scene: building, performing, or editing the layer of moving-air, gust, and breeze sounds separately from dialogue, Foley, and other effects.
fields.plain_english: This is when a sound editor focuses on just the wind for a scene. They build or record the moving-air and gust sounds on their own layer, apart from all the other sounds.
fields.purpose_function: Handling wind on its own pass lets the team place, shape, and mix gusts precisely, so the weather feels right without covering dialogue or other effects.
fields.practical_application: For an outdoor scene, an editor makes a wind pass, laying in steady breeze beds and timed gusts that swell on wide shots and ease back under close dialogue.
common_mistakes: Letting wind cover dialogue instead of easing it under speech.
Using one static wind loop with no gusts, so it sounds fake and flat.
Not matching wind level and motion to what the picture shows, such as trees, hair, or dust.
Building wind so busy that it clashes with music and other effects.
scenario_contexts: Creating weather for an outdoor dialogue scene.
Adding gusts to a storm or desert sequence.
Building an eerie wind bed for a tense, empty location.

sources: Yewdall, Practical Art of Motion Picture Sound
Wyatt & Amyes, Audio Post Production for Television and Film

fields.definition: A Foley or spot sound effect reproducing the sound of a window being shut: typically the slide or swing of the sash, the contact with the frame, and the final thud or rattle of glass and hardware settling.
fields.plain_english: This is the sound effect of a window being closed. It usually includes the slide of the window, the bump as it meets the frame, and a small rattle of the glass.
fields.purpose_function: It syncs a believable sound to the on-screen action of shutting a window, grounding the moment and supporting continuity and a sense of space.
fields.practical_application: A Foley artist performs the move on a matching window prop, or an editor cuts a library window-close effect, timing the frame contact exactly to the picture.
common_mistakes: Missing sync, so the sound lands before or after the sash actually meets the frame.
Using a heavy slam when the picture shows a gentle close, or the reverse.
Forgetting the small glass or latch rattle that makes it read as a window, not a door.
Ignoring the room's acoustics, so the effect sits outside the scene's space.
scenario_contexts: Covering an actor shutting a window in a drama.
Sealing off street noise before a quiet interior scene.
Marking a character closing off from the outside world.

sources: Ament, The Foley Grail: The Art of Performing Sound for Film, Games, and Animation
Viers, The Sound Effects Bible

fields.definition: A Foley or spot sound effect reproducing the operation of a window's fastening mechanism: the click, snap, or metallic clunk of the latch or lock engaging or releasing.
fields.plain_english: This is the small click or clunk of a window latch, the catch that locks a window shut. It is the sound of that catch snapping open or closed.
fields.purpose_function: It adds a precise mechanical detail that confirms a window is being secured or freed, reinforcing the action and the character's intent.
fields.practical_application: A Foley artist works a real latch or a stand-in metal prop to picture, or an editor cuts a library latch click, placing it exactly on the hand movement.
common_mistakes: Placing the click off the exact frame of the hand action.
Using a latch that sounds too large or heavy for the window shown.
Skipping the latch detail, so the window action feels incomplete.
Letting the click sit too loud and jump out of the scene.
scenario_contexts: A character locking a window before leaving a room.
Building tension as someone quietly unlatches a window to sneak in.
Detailing a period window's hardware in a drama.

sources: Ament, The Foley Grail: The Art of Performing Sound for Film, Games, and Animation
Viers, The Sound Effects Bible

fields.definition: A Foley or spot sound effect reproducing the sound of a window being opened: the release of the latch, the slide or swing of the sash, frame friction, and any squeak or glass movement.
fields.plain_english: This is the sound effect of a window being opened. It can include the latch letting go, the window sliding or swinging up, and a squeak or rattle as it moves.
fields.purpose_function: It matches sound to the on-screen act of opening a window and often cues a change in space, such as outside air, noise, or light entering.
fields.practical_application: A Foley artist performs the slide and friction on a window prop, or an editor cuts a library effect, then may bring up exterior ambience as the window opens.
common_mistakes: Not raising the outside ambience as the window opens, so the space does not change.
Mismatching a sliding-window sound to a swinging casement window, or the reverse.
Poor sync between the squeak or slide and the picture.
Overplaying the squeak, so it distracts from the scene.
scenario_contexts: A character opening a window to let in air or listen outside.
Revealing street or nature sounds as a window opens.
Building suspense as someone slowly opens a window to escape or intrude.

sources: Ament, The Foley Grail: The Art of Performing Sound for Film, Games, and Animation
Viers, The Sound Effects Bible

fields.definition: A hard sound effect of wood striking another surface: a sharp, resonant knock, crack, or thud whose tone depends on the wood's size, density, and hollowness, used for hits, collisions, and breaks.
fields.plain_english: This is the sound of wood hitting something, a knock, crack, or thud. How it sounds depends on how big, hard, or hollow the wood is.
fields.purpose_function: It gives on-screen wooden collisions, blows, and breaks a believable, weighty hit, and is often layered to build bigger crashes and destruction.
fields.practical_application: A designer or Foley artist records or cuts wood knocks and cracks, then may layer and pitch them under a fight hit, a falling crate, or a splintering door.
common_mistakes: Using a hollow, light knock where the picture shows heavy, solid timber.
Forgetting to layer low end when a big, weighty impact is needed.
Reusing the same wood hit repeatedly, so it sounds fake.
Sync drift between the visible contact and the hit.
scenario_contexts: A fist or body hitting a wooden door or table in a fight.
A wooden crate or piece of furniture falling and landing.
Building a splintering, breaking-wood effect for destruction.

sources: Viers, The Sound Effects Bible
Sonnenschein, Sound Design: The Expressive Power of Music, Voice and Sound Effects in Cinema
Yewdall, Practical Art of Motion Picture Sound

fields.definition: Foley footsteps performed or edited to match a character walking on a wood floor: the firm, slightly resonant, sometimes creaky footfalls whose tone reflects solid or hollow boards underfoot.
fields.plain_english: These are footstep sounds made to match someone walking on a wooden floor. They sound firm and a little hollow, and sometimes the boards creak.
fields.purpose_function: They match a character's movement to the wood surface shown on screen, keeping footsteps in sync and grounding the character in a believable space.
fields.practical_application: A Foley artist walks on a wood surface in the studio, matching each step to the actor's weight and shoes, or an editor cuts wood-floor footstep library takes to picture.
common_mistakes: Steps that drift out of sync with the actor's feet.
Using a hard shoe sound when the character is barefoot or in soft shoes.
Matching a hollow, boomy floor to a shot that shows solid ground, or the reverse.
Even, robotic steps that ignore the actor's real weight and rhythm.
scenario_contexts: Covering an actor walking across a wooden room in a drama.
Adding creaky steps to build tension in a quiet house.
Matching footstep tone to a period wooden interior.

sources: Ament, The Foley Grail: The Art of Performing Sound for Film, Games, and Animation
Yewdall, Practical Art of Motion Picture Sound
